Supervisor's note, week six
Gurpreet has struggled to start the monthly compliance report, usually beginning the night before. Two weeks ago we tried a new approach. Each evening she sets up her desk before leaving: file open, checklist printed. Each morning she commits to five minutes only.
I also told her the past late reports are behind us. No need to apologise again.
This month she began on the 3rd, not the 27th. She told me, "Once I forgave myself for the last ones, the dread got smaller." She looked relaxed at her desk today, which I haven't seen before.
Next month we'll keep the same routine.
Lakshmi

qa.q: On which day did Gurpreet begin the report this month?
qa.a: On the 3rd, not the 27th.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet feel once past late reports were forgiven?
qa.a: She felt the dread get smaller, and looked relaxed at her desk.

qa.q: Which parts of the routine made starting easier?
qa.a: Setting up the desk each evening, committing to five minutes each morning, and letting go of past late reports.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi feel about the change?
qa.a: Lakshmi seems pleased and encouraged, noticing Gurpreet relaxed for the first time.

grounding: Shows a supervisor's note on an employee starting with five minutes, a workspace set up the night before and forgiveness for past delays.

Dear Usha Bua,
Thank you for the fountain pen! I've already used it for my science notebook. Ma'am held it up in class today as an example of "perfect notes". Everyone clapped.
Papa says I'm the only child in the family who never makes mistakes. Mummy shows my copies to the neighbours. When I get full marks, Papa takes me for ice cream. I like that.
I rewrite a page if there's even one smudge. It takes ages, but it's worth it.
Sometimes I get a funny tight feeling when I think about the half-yearly exam. What if I'm not perfect? Then what?
But mostly I'm proud. Come for Diwali?
Your Pradeep

qa.q: What did Usha Bua give Pradeep?
qa.a: A fountain pen.

qa.q: What does Pradeep's tight feeling about the exam suggest?
qa.a: Underneath the pride, Pradeep feels afraid of not being perfect and of what might happen then.

qa.q: What could the adults around Pradeep do differently at this stage?
qa.a: Praise effort and learning, not just flawless results, and show love is not tied to being perfect.

qa.q: How might Usha Bua feel reading about the rewritten pages?
qa.a: Usha Bua might feel proud but also a little worried about the pressure Pradeep is under.

grounding: Shows a teen praised for perfect notes and marks, proud of the standard, with a hidden fear of not being perfect.

passage:
Deepak, you asked why I'm so fussy about my notebooks? It started in Class 8. My handwriting was so neat that my teacher said, "Parul, you're a perfectionist. That's a gift." After that, every report card said "Flawless work." At home, my parents beamed. My grandmother told everyone I was the clever one.
So I made sure I was always flawless. I felt safe when I was perfect. Like everyone loved me more.
It felt like a strength. Honestly, it still does.
But sometimes, at night, I lie awake thinking about one small mistake I might have made. And I feel scared, like all that love depends on it. Weird, right? That's me. The girl with the perfect notebooks.

qa.q: What did Parul's teacher say was a gift?
qa.a: Being a perfectionist.

qa.q: What does Parul feel while lying awake at night?
qa.a: Parul feels scared that one small mistake could cost the love and praise that come with being perfect.

qa.q: What could help Parul see her worth differently?
qa.a: Hearing from the adults around her that they love her for who she is, not only for flawless work.

qa.q: How might Deepak see Parul's fussiness now that she has explained it?
qa.a: Deepak may understand it as fear rather than just neatness, and feel sympathetic.

grounding: Shows a teen whose praised perfection feels like a strength but hides fear that love depends on being flawless.

passage:
Class 8: Tarun's teacher held up his notebook. "This is how every notebook should look!" At home, his father framed his certificate. Tarun felt warm all over.
Class 9: Tarun rewrote pages at the slightest smudge. His friend Nilesh laughed. "Yaar, it's just homework." Tarun said, "It has to be perfect." He liked how his parents smiled at his report cards.
Class 10: Before the prelims, Tarun couldn't sleep. He kept imagining a less-than-perfect mark, his father's face falling. "What if they're disappointed?" he asked Nilesh, and his voice cracked. Nilesh stopped laughing.

qa.q: What did Tarun's father frame?
qa.a: His certificate.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling before the prelims?
qa.a: Tarun felt anxious and scared, afraid his parents would be disappointed if he wasn't perfect.

qa.q: What turning point could help Tarun now?
qa.a: Telling his parents or a teacher about the fear, and hearing that their love doesn't depend on perfect marks.

qa.q: What might Nilesh feel when Tarun's voice cracks?
qa.a: Nilesh probably feels surprised and concerned, realising Tarun's perfectionism is about fear, not neatness.

grounding: Shows a teen whose praised perfection grows over years into a hidden fear that love depends on being flawless.

passage:
In the small town of Kalimpong, Rekha sat at the back of the maths class. When the teacher asked a question, Rekha knew the answer. But she didn't raise her hand. What if she was wrong?
In her notebook, the page was grey with rubbed-out numbers. She'd erased the same sum four times.
At lunch, her friend Tenzin asked, "Why didn't you answer? You always know."
"I wasn't sure."
"You were sure. I saw your notebook."
Rekha shrugged. Last week she'd got one question wrong in the unit test and felt sick the whole evening, lying awake. It felt like the mark was about her, not the sum.

qa.q: How many times had Rekha erased the same sum?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling when she didn't raise her hand?
qa.a: She felt afraid of being wrong, as if any mistake would say something bad about her.

qa.q: What small step could help Rekha?
qa.a: Raising her hand once even when not totally sure, and talking to a teacher she trusts about the fear.

qa.q: How might Tenzin see Rekha's silence?
qa.a: Tenzin is puzzled and a bit worried, knowing Rekha knew the answer.

grounding: Shows a teen erasing and rewriting, avoiding answers unless certain, and feeling sick over one wrong question.

passage:
In Copenhagen, Felix was the best at chemistry in his class. But he'd stopped answering questions in lessons. His lab book was full of crossed-out lines and rewritten sentences.
On Tuesday he made a tiny mistake in a calculation, a decimal in the wrong place. The teacher said, "Small slip, Felix." The class moved on.
Felix didn't. He felt sick all afternoon. At football practice, Anders asked what was wrong.
"I made a mistake in chemistry."
"So? Everyone does."
"Not me. I can't."
Anders looked at him for a long moment. "Felix, it was a decimal. You're allowed to be human."

qa.q: What mistake did Felix make?
qa.a: A decimal in the wrong place.

qa.q: What was Felix feeling after the tiny mistake?
qa.a: He felt sick and anxious all afternoon, as if the mistake threatened his worth.

qa.q: What could help Felix at this stage?
qa.a: Talking to his teacher or a counsellor about the fear, and practising small, low-stakes mistakes.

qa.q: How does Anders see Felix's reaction?
qa.a: Anders seems surprised and concerned, reminding Felix that making mistakes is human.

grounding: Shows a teen who rewrites everything, stops answering unless certain and feels sick over a tiny error, as mistakes threaten his worth.
